projects.title: Structural Characterization of Pathological Inclusions in Alzheimer's Disease
description: In Alzheimer's disease, the proteins amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau aggregate into fibrils that accumulate in brain tissue. Antibodies that clear amyloid plaques now slow cognitive decline in early disease, but researchers do not yet know how the fibrils form and change as the disease advances. Fibril structure may hold part of the answer, because one protein can fold into more than one fibril form, and the forms may damage tissue differently. Current methods cannot measure fibril structure where the fibrils sit. PET and MRI image the whole brain, but at a resolution far too coarse for fibril structure. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and solid-state NMR resolve fibrils in atomic detail, but only after the fibrils are purified from tissue, so the measurement loses the position of a fibril in the brain.

Scanning X-ray microdiffraction keeps that position, because it measures fibril structure inside thin sections of tissue. A synchrotron X-ray beam a few micrometers wide steps across the section and records a diffraction pattern at successive positions, so the patterns form a map of the section. Recovering fibril structure from the patterns poses an inverse problem with a weak signal, because the surrounding tissue scatters far more strongly than the fibrils and the detector adds noise. With neuropathologists at Massachusetts General Hospital and biophysicists at Brookhaven National Laboratory, we develop statistical signal processing and machine learning methods that separate the fibril signal from the tissue background and classify the patterns as Aβ, tau or tissue. We compare the fibril signal with diffraction patterns calculated from cryo-EM and solid-state NMR structures, and we map protein accumulation and tissue loss across disease stages. We aim to identify which fibril forms appear as tissue degenerates, so that future treatments could target those forms.

projects.title: Multi-omic Risk Stratification in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) narrows the airways and destroys the walls of the air sacs (emphysema), and it ranks among the leading causes of death worldwide. Treatment options have grown over the past decade and now include biologic drugs and valves placed in the airways to reduce lung volume. Clinicians still choose among the options with coarse measures, such as a spirometry value that summarizes lung function in one number and a CT score of total emphysema. Such measures describe the lung as a whole, so they show neither the failing lung region nor the biological process behind the damage.

We link molecular measurements in blood to damage in specific regions of the lung, so that a blood test can point to both the process and the region. The data come from the COPDGene study, which follows a large cohort of current and former smokers for about ten years with chest CT, spirometry, blood RNA sequencing and plasma proteomics. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) groups genes and proteins into modules of co-expressed molecules, and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) relates the modules to emphysema in lung regions defined on CT. A high-dimensional causal mediation model then tests which plasma proteins carry the effect of smoking on emphysema progression. We develop a multi-omic risk score from the proteins this model selects, as a weighted sum of protein levels from a routine blood draw. We design the score to rank patients by risk of lung-function decline, emphysema progression, exacerbations and death. The proteins in the score should also indicate the lung regions and pathways behind that risk, so that treatment could begin before the disease destroys more lung tissue.
